issues.legal_issue: A party alleging that the person named as purchaser in a sale deed was only a benamidar must prove that allegation by definite evidence, assessed in light of the relevant circumstances.
material_facts: The plaintiffs alleged that a house purchased in the wife’s name had in reality been purchased by her husband with his own funds.
The husband did not specifically testify that he paid the purchase price from his personal funds; his admitted assets and income indicated limited financial means.
Evidence indicated that the wife had resources of her own, and a later deed executed by her recited that she had incurred debts to help fund the purchase.
The husband’s involvement in negotiations, payment of part of the price, possession of the title deed, and later mortgages were not conclusive proof that he was the real purchaser.

There was no evidence establishing a motive for putting the house in the wife’s name, while municipal and other evidence supported the wife’s and, after her death, her daughter’s dealings with the property as owners.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiffs failed to prove that the wife was a benamidar and not the real purchaser. The Court affirmed the High Court’s decision and dismissed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The burden of proving a benami transaction rests on the person asserting it and must be discharged by definite legal evidence, either directly proving the transaction or establishing circumstances that unerringly support the inference. The named purchaser has an initial presumption in favour of the apparent state of affairs. The essential issue is the parties’ intention. Relevant circumstances include the source of the purchase money, possession and use of the property, motive, the parties’ positions and relationship, custody of title deeds, and their later conduct; these indicia are not exhaustive, and the source of the purchase money is the most important. No earlier case is relied on for this principle. In discussing a prior execution proceeding, the Court referred to section 13 of the Evidence Act and Order 21, Rule 103 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

rule.if: civil_title_suit and benami_transaction_alleged and (purchase_money_came_from_apparent_purchaser or apparent_purchaser_had_independent_means or ownership_conduct_supported_apparent_purchaser) and (alleged_beneficiary_lacked_means or no_definite_evidence_of_benami)

predicates.civil_title_suit: A party seeks a determination of title to property in a civil suit.
predicates.benami_transaction_alleged: A party alleges that the person named as purchaser in a property transaction was not the real purchaser.
predicates.purchase_money_came_from_apparent_purcha: Evidence indicates that the purchase money came from the person named as purchaser.
predicates.apparent_purchaser_had_independent_means: Evidence indicates that the person named as purchaser had resources of their own.
predicates.ownership_conduct_supported_apparent_pur: Possession, records, or dealings with the property support the named purchaser’s ownership.
predicates.alleged_beneficiary_lacked_means: Evidence indicates that the person alleged to be the real purchaser had limited means to fund the purchase.
predicates.no_definite_evidence_of_benami: The party alleging benami does not produce definite evidence directly proving it or circumstances unerringly supporting that inference.

issues.definition: In a civil title suit, when benami is alleged but the purchase funding or ownership conduct supports the named purchaser, or the alleged beneficiary lacked means or definite proof is absent, the allegation is not proved.

issues.legal_issue: A prior decision on a property claim in execution proceedings is not conclusive proof of ownership in a later suit when the deciding court could not try that suit and the decision is outweighed by other evidence.
material_facts: A person claiming ownership applied in execution proceedings to have the disputed house treated as her exclusive property, but the application was dismissed on a finding that she was a benamidar.
The decision was affirmed on appeal, but the court that made the original decision was not competent to decide the later suit.
The claimant died a few months after her appeal was dismissed, before the time for bringing a suit under Order 21, Rule 103 had expired.

The Court considered the execution decision on the assumption that it was admissible under section 13 of the Evidence Act, but found it inconclusive and outweighed by other evidence and the probability that the claimant had supplied the purchase money.
issues.conclusion: The prior execution decision was not conclusive proof that the claimant was a benamidar; even assuming it was admissible, it was outweighed by the other evidence.
issues.legal_principle: The Court noted that the execution decision did not operate as res judicata because the court that made it was not competent to try the later suit. Assuming without deciding that the decision was admissible under section 13 of the Evidence Act, it remained inconclusive in light of the other evidence. The Court also considered the claimant’s death before the limitation period for a suit under Order 21, Rule 103 had expired.

rule.if: later_title_suit and prior_execution_claim_decision and deciding_court_could_not_try_later_suit and claimant_died_before_followup_suit_period_expired and other_evidence_outweighed_prior_decision

predicates.later_title_suit: A party brings a later civil suit to establish ownership of property.
predicates.prior_execution_claim_decision: An earlier decision in execution proceedings rejected a person's claim to ownership of the property.
predicates.deciding_court_could_not_try_later_suit: The court that made the execution decision was not competent to decide the later suit.
predicates.claimant_died_before_followup_suit_perio: The person whose claim was rejected died before the period for bringing a follow-up suit had expired.
predicates.other_evidence_outweighed_prior_decision: The evidence in the later case supports a different conclusion more strongly than the earlier execution decision.

issues.definition: When the specified earlier execution decision is followed by a title suit, the deciding court lacked competence to try that suit, the claimant died before the follow-up period expired, and other evidence outweighs the decision, the earlier decision is not conclusive proof of ownership.

issues.legal_issue: A judgment in an earlier proceeding cannot be used against a person who was not a party to that proceeding to establish that person’s ownership of the disputed property.
material_facts: A judgment arose from an earlier rent suit concerning a shop attached to the disputed house.
The person whose ownership was relevant in the later dispute was not a party to that rent suit.
issues.conclusion: The earlier rent-suit judgment could not be used against the person who was not a party to those proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the judgment could not be used against a person who was not a party to the proceedings. No provision or earlier case was cited for this point.

predicates.later_ownership_dispute: A later proceeding concerns ownership of property.
predicates.prior_judgment_from_other_proceeding: A party offers a judgment from an earlier, separate proceeding as evidence in the later dispute.
predicates.person_against_whom_judgment_is_offered_: The person against whom the earlier judgment is offered did not participate as a party in that proceeding.

issues.definition: When an earlier judgment is offered against a person who was not a party to that proceeding in a later ownership dispute, it cannot be used against that person.
